analysis.one_liner: Reverses the top income tax cut from 35% back to 39.6% and puts the money into college aid.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its referral to the Senate Finance Committee and died without a vote or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Mark Dayton proposed undoing the portion of the 2001 tax cut that lowered the top income tax rate from 39.6% to 35%, which applies to the highest incomes. The revenue from that reversal would, in the bill's words, go to a $6 billion boost to the Montgomery GI Bill over ten years, full funding of Pell Grants as authorized for fiscal 2004, and a doubling of funding for Perkins Loans, Federal Work-Study, and Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grants. The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: College students, veterans using GI Bill education benefits, and low- and middle-income families relying on federal grants, loans, and work-study jobs would gain from the increased education funding. The bill raises the money by restoring the top individual income tax rate to 39.6%, which applies to the highest earners.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students, veterans, and low-income college families

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the reduction in the top tax rate, raising it from 35% to 39.6% for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2003.
Expresses the sense of the Senate that the added revenue should improve Montgomery GI Bill benefits by $6 billion over ten years.
Directs the revenue to fully fund Pell Grants at fiscal 2004 authorized amounts and double funding for Perkins Loans, Federal Work-Study, and Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grants.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers in the top income tax bracket, who would pay the 39.6% rate instead of 35% on their highest income.

drawbacks.text: Raising the top rate from 35% to 39.6% would increase taxes on the highest earners, which critics of the 2001 rate cuts' reversal argued would slow investment and job growth.

The education spending side of the bill is only a 'sense of the Senate' — a statement of opinion with no legal force — so Congress could have collected the tax increase without directing the money to GI Bill or student aid programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a higher top tax rate for materially more education aid, but its design is weak: only the tax change is binding, while the education spending is a non-binding statement, leaving the two halves unconnected. Even so, the core trade-off — top earners pay more, students and veterans get more — is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the bill expired when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Dayton introduced the bill on May 13, 2004.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No committee action, floor vote, or cosponsor followed, and the bill died at the end of the 108th Congress in January 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Top-bracket taxpayers kept the reduced 35% rate, and no new revenue was redirected to education or GI Bill programs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Top-bracket taxpayers kept their tax cut

for.name: Sen. Mark Dayton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, leaving it to die without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: One Democrat sponsored the bill, no cosponsors from either party joined, and no vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape is not visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have restored the 39.6% top income tax rate, ending the reduction to 35% for the highest earners. Because the bill died, they kept the lower rate.
Doubled work-study, Perkins Loan, and SEOG funding and full Pell funding would have flowed to campuses and their students. None of the funding materialized.
